modelAnswer: Management control comprises all devices and systems managers use to ensure that the behaviours and decisions of their employees are consistent with the organization's objectives and strategies. It is concerned with strategy implementation (not formulation) and aims to make it reasonably likely that objectives will be achieved.
keyPoints: Consistent with organizational objectives and strategies
Focus on strategy implementation, not formulation
Aims for high probability (not certainty) of achieving objectives

prompt: State the three control problems that management controls address and give one short example for each.
modelAnswer: 1) Lack of direction – employees do not know what the organization wants (e.g. unclear priorities). 2) Motivational problems – employees know what is expected but do not want to do it because individual and organizational goals differ (e.g. shirking, fraud). 3) Personal limitations – employees want to but are not able to (e.g. lack of skills, training or information).

prompt: Explain the difference between diagnostic and interactive control systems according to Simons.
modelAnswer: Diagnostic control systems are formal feedback systems used to monitor outcomes and correct deviations from preset standards of performance on critical performance variables; managers use them by exception. Interactive control systems are formal systems top managers use to involve themselves regularly and personally in subordinates' decisions; they focus on strategic uncertainties, stimulate dialogue and learning, and allow new strategies to emerge.
keyPoints: Diagnostic: monitor critical performance variables against preset standards
Diagnostic: management by exception / feedback, corrective
Interactive: top management personally and regularly involved
Interactive: focus on strategic uncertainties, dialogue, learning / emergent strategy

prompt: Explain what behavioural displacement is and why it is a cost of management controls.
modelAnswer: Behavioural displacement occurs when a control system produces and encourages behaviours that are not consistent with the organization's objectives – typically because results measures are incongruent or incomplete, so employees optimize what is measured rather than what matters (e.g. quantity over quality). It is an indirect cost because the control itself causes harmful behaviour.
keyPoints: Caused by the control system itself (e.g. incongruent / incomplete measures)
Employees focus on what is measured, not what matters (example)
